Physics, and mechanics of objects

Between ages 9 and 12, children see significant progress in their understanding of intuitive and explicit physics, along with related advancements in their understanding of objects and their utilization of tools. In "physics" per se, a landmark is that by roughly age 11 most children succeed on conservation-of-volume problems (e.g same amount of a liquid but in a taller glass), recognizing that quantity remains constant despite perceptual changes in appearance 1. On balance-beam problems, the modal strategy shifts from the weight-only or distance-only rules common around age 9 (Rule I/II) to Rule III, where weight and distance are jointly coordinated; by the end of this window the distribution of rule use approaches the adult profile, reflecting reliable multi-dimensional integration in physical problem solving 2, 3. In trajectory prediction, younger children are easily captured by salient but irrelevant contextual features (e.g the relative location of objects), whereas by 1̃2 performance is much improved and, more importantly, a substantial fraction of responses reflect engagement of an "impetus" conception, applying rudimentary physics principles rather than purely perceptual strategies 4.

In terms of applied physics, the same shift from percept-bound to principle-based reasoning is visible when children explain and predict the behavior of familiar mechanical artifacts. Direct evidence is surprisingly sparse, but where it exists it points to clear structural change. When asked "how a bicycle works," children’s explanations between 6 and 8 years are relatively flat and largely descriptive (naming parts, focusing on visible motion), with a noticeable step-wise improvement around 8-9 and continued gains through 9-10 as they begin to invoke hidden force-transmission mechanisms (e.g., chains transferring pedal force to wheels, the role of gears in trading off speed and torque) 5. Similarly, across this window their reasoning about simple gear trains becomes more principled and generalizable: rather than treating each configuration as a new visual puzzle, older children increasingly extract and apply abstract rules about motion transmission (e.g., "adjacent gears rotate in opposite directions") and can justify speed differences in terms of gear-size ratios rather than surface features 6. Speculatively, these advances in mechanical reasoning are mirrored in tool choice and tool sequencing during problem solving: by  12, many children can pick or improvise tools based on leverage, force redirection, and mechanical advantage rather than trial-and-error exploration alone, and can mentally "run" simple mechanisms forward to anticipate downstream consequences. Taken together with the more formal understanding of conservation, balance, and trajectories described above, these developments suggest that between 9 and 12 the child’s mechanical world model is upgraded from a patchwork of local heuristics about specific devices at age 9 to something closer to a compact, compositional physics engine by age 12-one that can be flexibly deployed to explain, predict, and manipulate novel physical systems in a way that begins to resemble an adult’s principled grasp of the physical world.

Multisensory cue integration

Another interesting capability reflecting decentration in late childhood is multisensory (multimodal) cue integration, where children begin to move from relying on a single, salient cue to combining multiple, partially redundant cues in something like an uncertainty-weighted, Bayesian way. For example, one study found that no participants younger than 12 were able to optimally integrate binocular visual disparity and surface texture information to reduce their uncertainty in judging the slant of a surface 7, with 12-year-olds clearly remaining below adult levels. Similarly, in another study the integration of multiple cues for depth perception (integrating visual disparity and relative motion) does not emerge (as measured both in terms of task accuracy and associated sensory-fusion activity in cortex) until roughly age 11, and then shows protracted development thereafter 8. By contrast, size and orientation prediction for objects may become statistically optimal, approaching adult-like weighting of visual and haptic information, during this age window (perhaps during the first half) 9. Thus, compared to 9-year-olds who still tend to treat individual modalities or cues in isolation, 12-year-olds are beginning to construct a more integrated, reliability-sensitive, and uncertainty-aware multisensory world model, even though their cue fusion remains less efficient and less automatic than in adults.

Knowledge of object taxonomies and classification abilities

Between ages 9 and 12, the rule-based (explicit) categorization system undergoes a critical maturation phase ("maturation" as in the system’s efficiency and consistency of deployment) 10; while 9-year-olds often default to guessing when faced with complex classification tasks, 10- to 11-year-olds reach near-adult levels of consistency in applying rule-based strategies 11. This same period appears to mark the emergence of strategic flexibility, for instance the ability to switch between thematic and taxonomic classification modes based on task demands. Children begin distinguishing when to use associative clustering (associating dog-bone because they co-occur in stories) versus categorical clustering (associating dog-cat because both are mammals) 12, selecting the appropriate strategy for contexts like creative writing versus biology study; this is essentially the development of meta-cognitive control over different classification algorithms, allowing task-appropriate deployment of different representational schemes.

The nature of the features children use for taxonomic classification also transforms dramatically across this window. Between 9 and 12, there’s a steep increase in children’s tendency to classify objects based on intensive properties (intrinsic characteristics like material composition or state of matter) rather than extensive properties like shape or size 13. So a 12-year-old is much more likely than a 9-year-old to group a metal fork and metal can together as "metal objects" rather than grouping by superficial perceptual features. However, even the older children often rely on salient prototypes (like identifying "air" as the basis for grouping gases) rather than true abstract concepts, suggesting they’re still transitioning from instance-based to principle-based causal models, particularly in complex conceptual domains like matter and substance.

Viewed through multiple-systems accounts of category learning, late childhood is the period when the explicit, rule-based route reliably wins the arbitration against the implicit, similarity-based route, although the discovery of optimal rules for classification sees continued development. When irrelevant dimensions are salient or feedback is noisy, these children can still be captured by perceptual similarity or revert to guessing: compared with adults, 8-12-year-olds remain less able to suppress an irrelevant dimension during rule application and are more brittle when the correct rule requires coordinating multiple cues or switching midstream 14.

Motor control and tool use

Predictive manipulation shows a clear step-change. In precision grip-lift tasks (e.g lifting something with only the thumb and index finger), children progressively shift from corrective, feedback-heavy lifts to anticipatory grip-force scaling that matches object weight and friction before contact, with classic longitudinal work indicating that the core feedforward capacity reaches an adult-like range by about 8-11 15; related work on predictive motor ability indicates that performance is in the adult range by about 12 on tasks requiring forecasting and acting on a forthcoming state 16. In practical terms, 12-year-olds can time interceptive actions (e.g., catching, striking) with far less over-reliance on late feedback than 9-year-olds (with interceptive actions, for example, being near adult-level at 12 16), who are more easily derailed by occlusion, acceleration, or context shifts.

Complementing predictive manipulation, online corrections also improve rapidly across this window: studies of constant isometric force (where muscular force perfectly matches resistance, e.g when holding a heavy object steady) show reductions in output noise and much more adult-like reweighting of visual and somatosensory feedback 17, and evidence from developmental movement-perturbation paradigms shows that the speed and accuracy of rapid online corrections continue to improve rapidly across this window 18.

Graphomotor control (handwriting) also crosses an important threshold. Cross-sectional analyses show handwriting speed climbs steeply from 8 to 10 and then stabilizes through 12, while "graphic" drawing speed (non-word writing speed) continues to improve from 10 to 12 19, evidence that by 12 the motor program itself has become more fluent even when central linguistic load is held constant. Consistent with that picture, the influence of lexical frequency on stroke timing is prominent at 8 but largely disappears by  11 19, indicating reduced central bottlenecks and greater automatization of the peripheral motor routine.

Consistent with these advancements, the ability to use tools develops rapidly between 9 and 12, reflecting advance mechanical reasoning abilities 20; 12-year-olds can independently and proficiently use simple tools such as hammers, scissors, and screwdrivers, engage in complex crafts like jewelry-making and model building, and execute intricate drawing tasks with spatial precision that was not consistently achievable at age 9. Again reflecting rapidly advancing mechanical reasoning skills, tool use innovation (making a new functional tool to complete a task) moves from nascent (classically nascent at age 8) to reliable by 12 20, although age effects on tool innovation tasks persist until around young adulthood.

Essential for everyday function and skilled tool use, bimanual coordination becomes meaningfully more independent. At 12, children show smaller "circles-lines" interference (drawing different figures simultaneously with each hand) 21 and can better sustain asymmetric/rhythmic patterns without one hand being captured by the other’s dynamics, reflecting improved interhemispheric coordination and higher-level control policies. Nine-year-olds, by contrast, still exhibit strong spatial coupling and phase-locking in dual tasks. This recent study illustrates figure 1 (Figure). This recent study illustrates figure 2 (Figure).

By around age 12, the motor system has achieved near-adult precision and fluidity under familiar conditions: children can anticipate object dynamics, stabilize posture under shifting sensory inputs, and coordinate multi-joint and bimanual movements smoothly and deliberately. Fine motor sequences like handwriting or instrument fingering are automated and resilient to cognitive distraction, while gross motor actions like running, turning, and balancing are supported by mature cerebellar feedforward control and executive oversight. Yet some limitations remain. Under novel or highly time-critical conditions, predictive models are still less stable and adaptable than in adults, leading to greater variability in unpracticed coordination, fatigue-sensitive endurance, and fine force scaling. In essence, the 12-year-old possesses a well-calibrated, efficient control architecture, but one whose internal models and strength parameters are still fine-tuning toward the adult brain’s precision and robustness.

Conclusion

Inferred capabilities

Fully "decentralized" (can coordinate multiple dimensions at once); can now simulate multiple interacting material and geometric properties at once (e.g a bowling ball falling on top of a paper object, then rolling down a hill) in a way that is functionally relevant (e.g a pencil is thin and sturdy so it can fit in my hand and won’t bend)

Large repository of objects’ materials, components, and mechanicsm which are now explicitly defined (including causally and functionally defined) and reasoned against

?? Devising novel uses for objects (e.g using a mug to hold pens) ??

Fully concrete operational: now essentially operating with the core architecture for flexible and robust concrete/physical simulation ("physical common sense")

semantic categories of physical entities, causal schemas for interaction types, and probabilistic priors over outcomes have all become both densely populated and dynamically linked

by 12, many children can (a) infer latent mechanical structure (center of mass, torque, friction), (b) run counterfactuals on that latent structure ("what if it were heavier / what if there was no friction?"), (c) select and even manufacture tools to exploit that structure, and (d) physically execute the required manipulation with anticipatory control rather than trial-and-error brute force

Limitations

Quantitative precision and dynamic parameter estimation: their internal physics engine has the correct architecture but suboptimal parameters; needs some fine-tuning still.

Extracting hidden constraints from minimal data: adults can watch a complex mechanism briefly and infer latent degrees of freedom, friction properties, or load-bearing limits. This requires not just simulation but meta-learned priors about what physical variables matter in novel contexts. Kids overgeneralize or miss subtle cues.

Predicting edge cases and failure modes: Adult physical intuition shines in knowing when things will break, slip, or behave unexpectedly under stress. This comes from accumulated prediction errors (including long-horizon prediction errors); a 12-year-old hasn’t debugged their models on enough corner cases or long-horizon projects/observations.

Compositional generalization to novel physical systems: Consider how adults quickly grasp unfamiliar tools, sports equipment, or mechanical systems by composing known physical principles. This requires rich, well-factorized representations that transfer flexibly. Kids’ models are more brittle and context-bound.

Overall, 11-12 is when you have a functioning forward model but nowhere near the prediction accuracy, generalization bandwidth, or error-corrected priors of an adult; essentially the difference between a high-fidelity but narrowly trained simulator and a fully generalizable world model.
